s.t: The J. Geils Band singer Peter Wolf improvised the spoken intro to the live ‘Must of Got Lost’, then had to memorise it from a cassette in a hotel room.
s.src: The Boston Globe: 50 years later, Peter Wolf looks back at the famous ramble that birthed ‘Reputah the Beautah’
s.q: “I had to sit up in a hotel room with a cassette and try to memorize what I did, spontaneously,” he added in a recent phone interview. “The whole story.”

s.t: J. Geils Band drummer Stephen Jo Bladd shouted “Rapunzel!” when Peter Wolf paused to name the woman in the live ‘Must of Got Lost’ rap; Wolf answered “Reputah the Beautah”.
s.src: The Boston Globe: 50 years later, Peter Wolf looks back at the famous ramble that birthed ‘Reputah the Beautah’
s.q: Drummer Stephen Jo Bladd shouted "Rapunzel!" when Wolf paused to name her, and Wolf answered with "Reputah the Beautah."

s.t: After the live album came out, fans began shouting “Reputah the Beautah!” at J. Geils Band shows, which singer Peter Wolf called “the most unusual thing”.
s.src: The Boston Globe: 50 years later, Peter Wolf looks back at the famous ramble that birthed ‘Reputah the Beautah’
s.q: After the album came out, audiences shouted "Reputah the Beautah!" or "Rapunzel!" at the band's shows. Wolf called this "the most unusual thing."

s.t: The live ‘Must of Got Lost’ never became a radio hit, but Boston DJ Maxanne Sartori recalls that “Detroit somehow got the word that Boston had played it”.
s.src: The Boston Globe: 50 years later, Peter Wolf looks back at the famous ramble that birthed ‘Reputah the Beautah’
s.q: "It didn't become a hit on the radio. Detroit somehow got the word that Boston had played it."

f.t: The band began as an acoustic blues trio called Snoopy and the Sopwith Camels: John Geils on guitar, Danny Klein on bass and Richard ‘Magic Dick’ Salwitz on harmonica.
f.q: Originally named Snoopy and the Sopwith Camels, the group was an acoustic blues trio with Geils on guitar, bassist Danny Klein ("Dr. Funk"), and harmonica player Richard Salwitz ("Magic Dick").

f.t: Before fronting the band, he was an overnight DJ on Boston’s WBCN, where Charles Daniels, ‘The Master Blaster’, nicknamed him ‘Woofa Goofa’; he chose the band over overnights.
f.src: Museum of Modern Music (MMONE): Peter Wolf, WBCN DJ
f.q: Charles Daniels, nicknamed "The Master Blaster," called Wolf "Woofa Goofa" … Sam Kopper recalled that "we had to give Peter the option: you can either do overnights or you can become a rock star."

f.t: In The Rolling Stone Record Guide (1979), critic Dave Marsh called their harmonica player Richard ‘Magic Dick’ Salwitz possibly “the best white musician to ever play blues harmonica”.
f.q: In The Rolling Stone Record Guide (1979), critic Dave Marsh called him possibly "the best white musician to ever play blues harmonica."

f.t: At a Boston Common show on 17 August 1971, the Allman Brothers Band named them its favourite local band; both later played the Fillmore East’s last show.
f.q: On August 17, 1971, at a show on the Boston Common, The Allman Brothers Band named The J. Geils Band as its favorite local band. Both bands later played the last show at the Fillmore East prior to the venue's closing.

f.t: Bloodshot first came out on red vinyl with matching red 1950s-style Atlantic labels; they kept vintage labels, in a new colour, on every later Atlantic album.
f.q: The original U.S. copies of Bloodshot were distributed in red vinyl instead of the customary black, with matching red 1950s style Atlantic Records labels. The band would continue to use these vintage-style Atlantic labels, in different colors with each album release
